questions.question: Which statement about the elements of an R list, created with `list()`, is correct?
options: They may differ in type, length and structure, each keeping its own type.
They may have any length, but R converts them all to one shared common type.
They may differ in type, but they must all have the same length.
They may be vectors of any type, but not matrices or other lists.

questions.question: `data.frame(a = c(1, 2), b = c("x", "y", "z"))` stops with the error `arguments imply differing number of rows: 2, 3`, while `list(a = c(1, 2), b = c("x", "y", "z"))` runs. Why does the list call succeed?
options: `list()` recycles `c(1, 2)` to length 3 before it stores the element `a`.
`list()` keeps only the first two values of `b`, so both elements have length 2.
List elements may have different lengths; the columns of a data frame may not.
`list()` joins the five values into one vector, so no lengths are compared.

questions.question: For a list `l`, R reports that `length(l)` is `3`. Which conclusion about `l` is justified?
options: `l` holds exactly three single values in total, one per element.
`l` has three elements, each of any length or structure.
`l` has three elements, and they all share one type.
`l` has three elements, none of which is itself a list.

questions.question: After `x <- list(2.5, "b", FALSE); y <- c(2.5, "b", FALSE)`, what does `c(typeof(x), typeof(y))` return?
options: `[1] "character" "character"`
`[1] "list" "list"`
`[1] "double"    "character"`
`[1] "list"      "character"`

questions.question: `str(list(10L, "b", FALSE))` prints one line for each element of the list, with a type abbreviation. Which abbreviations appear, in order?
options: `int`, `chr`, `logi`
`chr`, `chr`, `chr`
`num`, `chr`, `logi`
`int`, `chr`, `int`

questions.question: What does `names(list(5, "a"))` return?
options: `NULL`
`character(0)`

questions.question: Which code creates the same list as `list(A = "x", B = 2)`, with the same elements, types and names?
options: `l <- list("x", 2); names(l) <- c("A", "B")`
`l <- list("x", 2); names(l) <- c("B", "A")`

questions.question: When R prints the list `list(4, "b")`, which label appears on the line directly above `[1] "b"`?
After `x <- c(c(2L, 4L, 6L), "k"); y <- list(c(2L, 4L, 6L), "k")`, what does `c(length(x), length(y))` return?
Which call creates a list with exactly two elements: `id`, holding the string `"s1"`, and `score`, holding the three numbers 6, 7 and 8?
options: `list(id = "s1", score = 6, 7, 8)`
`list(id = "s1", score = c(6, 7, 8))`
`list(id = "s1", list(score = c(6, 7, 8)))`

questions.question: `v <- c(1, 2, 3); v * 2` returns `[1] 2 4 6`, but `l <- list(1, 2, 3); l * 2` stops with the error `non-numeric argument to binary operator`. Why?
options: A list stores numbers as text, so they need `as.numeric()` before any arithmetic.
Arithmetic needs an atomic vector; a list is not numeric, even with only numbers inside.
A list must have names for all of its elements before arithmetic can reach them.
`2` has length 1 and `l` has length 3, and lists do not recycle a shorter operand.

questions.question: `M <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), nrow = 2)` is a $2\times3$ matrix. Which statement correctly compares `c(M, 7)` and `list(M, 7)`?
options: Both keep `M` as a $2\times3$ matrix and add 7 next to it as a separate piece.
`c(M, 7)` adds 7 to `M` as an extra column; `list(M, 7)` has two elements.
Both give the seven numbers in a row, because a list also flattens a matrix.
`c(M, 7)` is a plain vector of 7 numbers; `list(M, 7)` holds the matrix and 7.

questions.question: Which description of what `str(list(a = 1, b = list(2, "z")))` prints for the element `b` is correct?
options: A line `List of 2` for `b`, then two indented lines for its elements: `num 2` and `chr "z"`.
A single line `List of 2` for `b`; `str()` does not show the elements of an inner list.
A single line `chr [1:2] "2" "z"` for `b`, since the inner values are combined into one type.
Two lines `num 2` and `chr "z"` at the same level as `a`, since `str()` flattens inner lists.

questions.question: What does `names(list(a = 1, 2, c = 3))` return?
What does `length(list(c(1, 2, 3, 4), list(5, 6, 7), "z"))` return?
For `df <- data.frame(x = c(1L, 2L, 3L), y = c("p", "q", "r"))`, what does `c(typeof(df), class(df))` return?
options: `[1] "character"  "data.frame"`
`[1] "list" "list"`
`[1] "integer"    "data.frame"`
`[1] "list"       "data.frame"`

questions.question: Which statement about the list `l <- list(c(1, "a"), 2)` is correct?
options: Its first element is the character vector `"1" "a"`, the second the double 2.
Its first element keeps the number 1 and the string `"a"`, each with its own type.
It has three elements, `1`, `"a"` and `2`, each keeping its own type.
It has two elements, and both are character, matching the string `"a"`.

questions.question: When can `c()` replace `list()` for collecting several objects, so that every value, type and piece stays exactly as it was?
options: Whenever every object gets a name, as in `c(n = "Ann", g = 8)`.
When all objects share one type and no piece must stay separate.
Whenever each object is a single value, as in `c("Ann", 8, TRUE)`.
Whenever all objects are numbers, even mixing integers and doubles.

questions.question: With `M <- matrix(c(4, 2, 3, 5), nrow = 2)`, one object should hold a firm's name `"Acme"`, its sales `c(12, 15, 11)` and the cost matrix `M`, each kept exactly as it is. Which call does this?
options: `list(name = "Acme", sales = c(12, 15, 11), cost = c(M))`
`c(name = "Acme", sales = c(12, 15, 11), cost = M)`
`list(name = "Acme", sales = c(12, 15, 11), cost = M)`
`data.frame(name = "Acme", sales = c(12, 15, 11), cost = M)`

questions.question: The outer list `list("p", list(3, 4))` contains a second, inner list. In R's printout of the outer list, which position label introduces the value `[1] 4`?
